hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to large fields of vibrant lime green, chartreuse, or bright yellow-green color. This chromatic feature manifests primarily in two configurations: as a smooth, out-of-focus background wash suggesting sunlit foliage, or as the textured surface of a foreground subject (e.g., a tennis ball, snake, or lizard). The green regions are highly saturated and typically create a strong chromatic contrast with adjacent areas of warm earth tones (orange, terracotta, rust, brown), black, or deep blue. The neuron is invariant to whether the green acts as the figure or the ground, as well as to the specific semantic content (birds, mammals, reptiles, or inanimate objects), provided the intense yellow-green hue is the dominant visual element. The activating green field typically occupies 40–90% of the image area, often surrounding or defining the boundaries of a sharply focused contrasting subject.
